desc:
Choose exactly one cell from every row of the matrix, so that the cells chosen in two consecutive rows never lie in the same column. (The columns of rows that are further apart may coincide.)

Return the smallest possible sum of the chosen values. The input always admits a valid choice: if the matrix has more than one row, it has more than one column.
hints: Let f[r][c] be the best sum for rows 0..r if row r uses column c. Which values of the previous row are allowed?
f[r][c] = matrix[r][c] + min over b ≠ c of f[r-1][b]. Computing the inner minimum from scratch for every c gives O(m · n2), which you can improve.

For a whole row f[r-1] only two numbers matter: its smallest value (at column i1) and the smallest value among the other columns. Column c ≠ i1 uses the smallest value, column i1 uses the second smallest.
editorial: The recurrence f[r][c] = matrix[r][c] + min over b ≠ c of f[r-1][b] follows from the fact that only the column of the previous row matters for the rule. To avoid scanning all other columns for each c, notice that the minimum of 'all except one' is the global minimum unless the excluded column is exactly the one holding the global minimum, in which case it is the second smallest value of the row.

So per row we find the smallest value (with its column) and the second smallest value in one pass, then fill the next row in O(n). The total is O(m · n) time and O(n) space. Care is needed for ties: if the smallest value occurs twice, the second smallest equals the smallest, which the 'smallest of the others' scan handles naturally. A single-row matrix is simply the minimum of that row.
